intro: Mangaluru is the port city of the Karnataka coast, where the Netravati and Gurupura rivers reach the Arabian Sea. In Bolar, its riverside quarter, a reader found two giant rain trees a few minutes' walk apart: one spreading over a lane behind a garden wall, its limbs lined with ferns, and one on the new riverside promenade carrying a wooden tree house in its limbs. We would like readers to tell us more about both.
meta_description: Two giant rain trees in Bolar, Mangaluru, sent by a reader: one over a lane, one with a tree house on the Netravati promenade, and how to find them.

trees.name: The Rain Tree of Bolar
trees.story:
A reader walking a lane in Bolar, the old riverside quarter of Mangaluru near where the Netravati meets the sea, stopped under this tree and sent us its photograph.

The picture shows why. A short trunk, far thicker than the power poles beside it, breaks almost at once into great dark limbs that run out sideways for metres before they turn up, and over them all spreads a crown wide enough to roof the lane, the wall and the garden behind it. Ferns grow all along the upper side of the limbs, the way they do on old trees on this wet coast, and the fine leaves let the sky through in a lace.

It has the build of a rain tree, Samanea saman, the South American giant planted along roads across South India for its shade, whose leaflets fold up before rain and at dusk. If you know it to be something else, tell us here.

We do not know its age, girth or who planted it. The reader sent no note, so the photograph is all we have, and it is enough to make the walk. Stand back on the lane to take in the whole spread of the crown.
trees.how_to_recognise: Behind a low garden wall on a lane in Bolar: a huge umbrella crown over a short, thick trunk, its fern-covered limbs spreading wide above an electricity transformer on a concrete plinth.
trees.access: Seen from the public lane where the reader stood; the garden behind the wall may be private.

trees.name: The Tree House Rain Tree of the Netravati Promenade

location.address: Netravati riverfront promenade, Bolar, Mangaluru, Karnataka

trees.story:
A reader walking the new riverside promenade in Bolar, where Mangaluru meets the Netravati, sent us this tree, and it is easy to see why they stopped.

The trunk is thick and leans towards the water, and low down it throws out one enormous limb almost level with the ground, reaching out over the planted beds towards the river before it turns up to the light. Above it the crown spreads in every direction, a wide roof of fine leaves that lets the grey sky through in lace. Someone thought the tree strong enough to carry a house, and a wooden tree house with a railed deck now sits in the fork, reached by a long timber stair. Beyond it the railway bridge crosses the river.

It has the build of a rain tree, Samanea saman, the South American shade tree planted across South India, whose leaflets fold up at dusk and before rain. If you know it to be something else, tell us here.

We do not know its age or girth, or who planted it. The reader sent no note, so the photograph is what we have. Another giant rain tree, the Rain Tree of Bolar, stands a few minutes' walk inland. Come at the end of the day and watch the leaves close over the river.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the riverside promenade: the big leaning tree with a wooden tree house and a long timber stair built into its limbs, one huge limb reaching out low towards the river.

question_meta: Two giant rain trees in Bolar, Mangaluru, sent by a reader: one over a lane, one with a tree house on the Netravati promenade, and how to find them.
question_answer: Two giant rain trees stand a few minutes apart in Bolar, Mangaluru: the Rain Tree of Bolar on a lane, seen from the street, and a rain tree carrying a tree house on the public Netravati riverfront promenade.
question_context: A reader walking in Bolar, the riverside quarter of Mangaluru on the Karnataka coast, sent us two trees. The first stands behind a garden wall on a lane, with an electricity transformer and a pair of power poles in front of it, and it dwarfs all of them: a short, very thick trunk splitting low into long, heavy limbs lined with ferns, under a wide flat umbrella of fine leaves. The garden may be private, but the whole tree is seen from the lane. The second is a few minutes' walk away on the new riverside promenade along the Netravati, free to walk, where a thick leaning trunk throws one huge limb out low towards the water and a wooden tree house with a long stair sits in its fork, the railway bridge behind. Both have the build of a rain tree, Samanea saman, the South American shade tree planted widely in South India, though we would like readers to confirm it. We have no age, girth or planting date for either yet; the reader's photographs are what put them on the map.

faq.q: Can I visit the rain trees of Bolar?
faq.a: Yes. The tree on the riverside promenade is on free public ground. The Rain Tree of Bolar stands behind a garden wall that may be private, but the whole tree is seen from the public lane.

faq.q: What kind of trees are they?
faq.a: Both have the build of a rain tree, Samanea saman: a massive trunk, long low limbs and a wide umbrella crown. A reader's photographs are all we have, so we ask visitors to confirm it.

faq.q: How old are the rain trees of Bolar?
faq.a: We do not know yet. No age, girth or planting date has reached us; if you know one, tell us on the tree's page.
